idiom_name: fp-ts Apply + getApplicativeValidation over Either with a Semigroup error
implementation_notes: The library realization: independent checks return Either<ReadonlyNonEmptyArray<E>, T> and sequenceT/sequenceS from Apply run under Either.getApplicativeValidation(semigroup), so every Left is concatenated instead of the first one winning. Choose it when the codebase already uses fp-ts and validation must be exhaustive; the trade-off is the higher-kinded encoding and the need to thread the validation instance consistently.
pitfalls: Using the default Either instance by accident is the classic bug: fail-fast and accumulating variants are both valid values of the same type.
Error order follows the chosen Apply instance; do not rely on source order when using a parallel Task or TaskEither instance.

variants.name: Native Promise.all + structured accumulator (concurrent)
variants.implementation_notes: The platform realization: Promise.all starts every independent effect concurrently and pairs the results positionally under a typed tuple, while accumulation is explicit - each producer resolves to a value or an error and the caller folds the settled results. Choose it when the effects are IO and exhausting them matters more than short-circuiting; the trade-off is that the type system does not distinguish fail-fast from accumulating usage.
pitfalls: Promise.all rejects on the first failure while the other effects keep running: the results of the successful ones are lost unless each call resolves to a result value instead of rejecting.
Tuple order is positional: `as const` keeps the tuple type, but reordering the array without reordering the destructuring still type-checks.
TypeScript cannot check independence - a missing await inside the array silently combines the Promise object instead of its value.
